extracted.intended_audience: general public, students, policymakers, and legal observers
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of statutory provisions, eligibility rules, judicially interpreted legal standards, and programmatic limits described in the Affordable Care Act (ACA) article. Focuses on concrete legal/policy requirements and the page's explanatory guidance about them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer mandate (threshold >50 employees)
rubrics_metrics.description: The employer mandate applies to employers of more than fifty where health insurance is provided only to the full-time workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes critics claimed this created a perverse incentive to hire part-timers; discussion includes empirical evidence about part-time and full-time job trends and that relatively few firms employ over 50 employees and most already offered insurance. The mandate context includes debate about reporting/administration costs and effects on marginal cost of the 50th worker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full-time worker definition (30 hours/week)
rubrics_metrics.description: Full-time worker defined as 30 hours-or-more per week (the 30-hour definition informed employer behavior).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article gives examples (some businesses and a state adding a 29-hour cap for part-time employees to reflect the 30-hour-or-more definition) and cites surveys indicating few companies shifted workforce hours; used in discussions of perverse incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medicaid expansion conditional funding (withholding of funds)
rubrics_metrics.description: ACA withheld all Medicaid funding from states declining to participate in the expansion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision was the basis of a Supreme Court challenge; the Court ruled that withholding all Medicaid funding for nonparticipating states was unconstitutionally coercive, holding states could opt out without losing preexisting Medicaid funding. The article describes how the ruling changed the practical scope of the expansion and subsequent CBO/JCT budget projections were updated to reflect states' opt-outs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual mandate constitutional basis (tax vs Commerce Clause)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court ruled the individual mandate was constitutional when viewed as a tax, although not under the Commerce Clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is reported as the holding in National Federation of Independent Business v. Sebelius; the article notes subsequent litigation and debates about the mandate's basis (including later arguments that elimination of the tax changes the constitutional analysis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Premium tax-credit subsidies availability on federal exchanges (King v. Burwell)
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal subsidies for health insurance premiums could be used in the 34 states that did not set up their own insurance exchanges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The June 25, 2015 Supreme Court decision in King v. Burwell (6–3) affirmed that subsidies are available on federal exchanges. The article places this as resolving a key question about subsidy eligibility across state-run versus federal-run exchanges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-sharing reduction (CSR) payments and appropriations constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Payments to insurers for cost-sharing reductions (CSRs) were challenged on the ground that Congress had not appropriated funds to pay for them; the legality of CSR payments was litigated and administrations later ceased payments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article recounts litigation (House v. Price and United States House of Representatives v. Azar) alleging CSRs were discretionary spending needing appropriation, the federal government's later cessation of payments, insurer premium effects (estimates of 20–30% increases for silver plans), and court findings about whether Congress authorized the program and spending. It notes insurer responses to the uncertainty and settlement outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: No cost-sharing for USPSTF grade A or B preventive services (section 2713)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 2713 of the ACA prohibits cost sharing for United States Preventive Services Task Force grade A or B recommended services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article links this provision to expanded access to zero-cost preventive care (examples include diabetes screenings) and estimates (e.g., 2.3 million of ~4.6 million undiagnosed adults with diabetes may have gained access to zero-cost preventive care). Used to illustrate ACA impacts on preventive services utilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subsidy eligibility exclusion for unauthorized immigrants
rubrics_metrics.description: ACA explicitly denies insurance subsidies to 'unauthorized (illegal) aliens'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit statutory eligibility limit; the article cites the provision and places it among coverage-eligibility rules discussed in the law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Members of Congress required to obtain coverage through exchanges or approved programs
rubrics_metrics.description: ACA requires members of Congress and their staffs to obtain health insurance either through an exchange or some other program approved by the law (such as Medicare), instead of using the insurance offered to federal employees (the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article states this as a specific provision affecting members of Congress and staff; it is presented as a transparency/accountability measure in the law's provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent Payment Advisory Board (IPAB) authority and statutory prohibitions
rubrics_metrics.description: IPAB was given the authority to recommend cost-saving changes to Medicare but was prohibited from recommending changes that would reduce payments before 2020, and prohibited from recommending changes in premiums, benefits, eligibility and taxes, or other changes that would result in rationing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article describes IPAB's narrowly circumscribed powers and cites these statutory prohibitions in the context of discussing criticisms and 'death panel' misconceptions. It explains what IPAB could and could not recommend and how that framed public debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment to False Claims Act re: administrative-disclosure immunity
rubrics_metrics.description: ACA updated a portion of the False Claims Act so that a subsection giving public officials immunity to qui tam lawsuits for false statements in 'administrative' disclosures is limited to federal disclosures (not state officials).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article references Graham County Soil & Water Conservation District v. United States ex rel. Wilson and explains the statutory change narrowing the earlier interpretation; presented as a legal/regulatory clarification effected by ACA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious/moral exemptions to contraceptive coverage (judicially recognized)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court (Burwell v. Hobby Lobby) ruled that employers with religious or moral objections can exclude contraceptive coverage from employee insurance; later cases (e.g., Little Sisters of the Poor) further addressed exemptions and injunctions affecting contraceptives and other services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article recounts the March 2012 and July 2020 litigation outcomes: Hobby Lobby allowed for-profit employers to exclude contraceptive coverage on religious grounds; Little Sisters of the Poor and subsequent district court rulings granted broader exemptions or injunctions and triggered government responses. The guidance includes majority and dissenting opinions and the practical effect of these rulings on coverage.
